nodes.name: Kernelization
nodes.statement: Given a (w.l.o.g.\ binarily encoded) instance $(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ of some parameterized problem $L$, a \emph{kernelization} for~$L$ produces in polynomial time an instance~$(x',k')$ satisfying: $(x',k') \in L \iff (x,k) \in L$ and $|x'| + k' \leq f(k)$ for some fixed computable function~$f(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: A kernelization maps $(x,k)$ in polynomial time to an equivalent $(x',k')$ with $|x'|+k'\le f(k)$.

nodes.name: Kernel
nodes.statement: In this way, kernelization can be thought of as a preprocessing procedure that reduces an instance to its ``computationally hard core" (\emph{i.e.},~the \emph{kernel}).

nodes.name: Size of a kernel
nodes.statement: The function~$f(k)$ is accordingly called the \emph{size} of the kernel, and it is typically the measure that one wishes to minimize.

nodes.name: Kernelization characterizes FPT
nodes.statement: Kernelization is a central concept in parameterized complexity not only as an important algorithmic tool, but also because it provides an alternative definition of \emph{fixed-parameter tractability} (\textnormal{FPT}{}): A parameterized problem is solvable in $f(k) \cdot |x|^{O(1)}$ time if and only if it has a kernel of size $g(k)$ for some arbitrary computable functions $f$ and $g$ only depending on the parameter~$k$~\cite{CaiCDF97}.
assumptions: $f$ and $g$ only depending on the parameter~$k$
conclusions: A parameterized problem is solvable in $f(k) \cdot |x|^{O(1)}$ time if and only if it has a kernel of size $g(k)$
equivalent_conditions: A parameterized problem is solvable in $f(k) \cdot |x|^{O(1)}$ time
it has a kernel of size $g(k)$
nodes.statement_short: A parameterized problem is FPT iff it has a kernel of some computable size.

nodes.name: No polynomial kernels unless NP in coNP/poly (Bodlaender et al.)
nodes.statement: The latter question was answered negatively by Bodlaender \emph{et al.}~\cite{BodlaenderDFH09} who used a lemma of Fortnow and Santhanam~\cite{FortnowS11} to show that various \textnormal{FPT}{} problems, \emph{e.g.}~\prob{Path} parameterized by the solution size, do not admit a polynomial-size kernel (or \emph{polynomial kernel} for short) unless $\textnormal{NP}{}\subseteq\textnormal{\textnormal{coNP}{}$/$poly}{}${} (which implies a collapse in the Polynomial Hierarchy to its third level).
nodes.statement_short: Path(k) and other FPT problems have no polynomial kernel unless NP is in coNP/poly.
nodes.origin_citation: Bodlaender, Downey, Fellows, Hermelin 2009; Fortnow & Santhanam 2011

nodes.name: Strict Kernel
nodes.statement: A strict kernelization for a parameterized problem $L$ is a polynomial-time algorithm that on input instance~$(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ outputs an instance~$(x',k')\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$, the \emph{strict kernel}, satisfying: \begin{inparaenum}[(i)] \item $(x, k) \in L \iff (x', k') \in L$, \item $|x'| \le f(k)$, for some function $f$, and \item $k' \le k + c$, for some constant $c$. \end{inparaenum} We say that $L$ admits a strict \emph{polynomial} kernelization if~$f(k)\in k^{O(1)}$.
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial-time equivalence-preserving map with output size $f(k)$ and parameter at most $k+c$; polynomial if $f(k)\in k^{O(1)}$.
nodes.label: def:strictPK

nodes.name: Strict kernels characterize FPT
nodes.statement: Finally, the equivalence with \textnormal{FPT}{} is preserved: A parameterized problem is solvable in $f(k) \cdot |x|^{O(1)}$ time if and only if it has a strict kernel of size $g(k)$.
conclusions: A parameterized problem is solvable in $f(k) \cdot |x|^{O(1)}$ time if and only if it has a strict kernel of size $g(k)$
equivalent_conditions: A parameterized problem is solvable in $f(k) \cdot |x|^{O(1)}$ time
it has a strict kernel of size $g(k)$

nodes.name: No strict polynomial kernel for Rooted Path (Chen, Flum, Müller)
nodes.statement: Chen, Flum, and M\"{u}ller~\cite{chen2011lower} showed that \prob{Rooted Path}, the problem of finding a path of length~$k$ in a graph that starts from a prespecified root vertex, has no strict polynomial kernel unless $\textnormal{P}{}\neq\textnormal{NP}{}${}.

nodes.name: No strict polynomial kernel for CNF-Sat (Chen, Flum, Müller)
nodes.statement: They also showed a similar result for \prob{CNF-Sat} parameterized by the number of variables.

nodes.name: Main theorem: no strict polynomial kernels unless P = NP
nodes.statement: Unless $\textnormal{P}{}=\textnormal{NP}{}${}, each of the following fixed-parameter tractable problems does not admit a strict polynomial kernel: \begin{compactitem} \item \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} and \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k \log n}; \item \pprob{Clique}{\Delta}{}, \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{tw}}{}, \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{bw}}{}, and \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{cw}}; \item \pprob{Biclique}{\Delta}{}, \pprob{Biclique}{\mathrm{tw}}{}, \pprob{Biclique}{\mathrm{bw}}{}, and \pprob{Biclique}{\mathrm{cw}}{}; \item \pprob{Colorful Graph Motif}{k} and \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|}{}; \item \pprob{Short NTM Computation}{k+|\Sigma|} and \pprob{Short NTM Computation}{k+|Q|}. \item \pprob{Short Binary NTM Computation}{k}{}; \end{compactitem} Herein, $k$~denotes the solution size, $n$~denotes the number of vertices in the graph, $\Delta$ denotes the maximum vertex degree in the graph, $\mathrm{tw}$, $\mathrm{bw}$, and $\mathrm{cw}$~denote the treewidth, bandwidth, and cutwidth of the graph, respectively, $T$~denotes the set of terminals, $|\Sigma |$~denotes the alphabet size, and~$|Q|$~denotes the number of states.
assumptions: Unless $\textnormal{P}{}=\textnormal{NP}{}${}
conclusions: each of the following fixed-parameter tractable problems does not admit a strict polynomial kernel
nodes.statement_short: Unless P=NP, Multicolored Path, Clique/Biclique under degree/width parameters, Colorful Graph Motif, Terminal Steiner Tree and Short NTM Computation have no strict polynomial kernel.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Logarithm base two

nodes.name: Parameter Diminisher
nodes.statement: A \emph{parameter diminisher} for a parameterized problem~$L$ is a polynomial-time algorithm that maps instances~$(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ to instances~$(x', k') \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ such that $(x, k) \in L \text{ if and only if } (x', k') \in L$ and $k' < k$.
differentia: $(x, k) \in L \text{ if and only if } (x', k') \in L$
also_stated_at: The main concept behind the new proof framework is that of a \emph{parameter diminisher}: an algorithm that is able to decrease the parameter value of any given instance by at least one in polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial-time map to an equivalent instance with strictly smaller parameter.
nodes.label: def:diminisher

nodes.name: Diminishable problem
nodes.statement: We call a parameterized problem~$L$~\emph{diminishable} if there is a parameter diminisher for $L$.
differentia: there is a parameter diminisher for $L$

nodes.name: Diminisher plus strict polynomial kernel implies P = NP
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \textnormal{NP}{}-hard and we have that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \textnormal{P}{}$, for some constant $c$. If $L$ is diminishable and admits a strict polynomial kernel, then $\textnormal{P}{}=\textnormal{NP}{}${}.
also_stated_at: It is not difficult to show that the existence of a parameter diminisher and a strict polynomial kernel for an \textnormal{NP}{}-hard parameterized problem implies $\textnormal{P}{}=\textnormal{NP}{}${}.
assumptions: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \textnormal{NP}{}-hard
$\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \textnormal{P}{}$, for some constant $c$
$L$ is diminishable and admits a strict polynomial kernel
nodes.statement_short: An NP-hard diminishable problem, polynomial for bounded parameter, with a strict polynomial kernel gives P=NP.
nodes.label: thm:diminisher

nodes.name: Proof idea of Theorem 2
nodes.statement:
The idea behind~\Cref{thm:diminisher} is to repeat the following two procedures until the parameter value drops below~$c$ (see \Cref{fig:dim} for an illustration). 
First, apply the parameter diminisher a constant number of times such that when, second, the strict polynomial kernelization is applied, the parameter value is decreased. The strict polynomial kernelization keeps the instances small, hence the whole process runs in polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: Alternate a constant number of diminisher applications with the strict kernel until the parameter drops below $c$.

nodes.name: Repeat two procedures
nodes.statement: The idea behind~\Cref{thm:diminisher} is to repeat the following two procedures until the parameter value drops below~$c$ (see \Cref{fig:dim} for an illustration).
nodes.statement_short: Iterate diminisher and kernel until parameter below $c$.

nodes.name: Diminish then kernelize
nodes.statement: First, apply the parameter diminisher a constant number of times such that when, second, the strict polynomial kernelization is applied, the parameter value is decreased.
nodes.statement_short: Apply diminisher constantly often, then the strict kernel, decreasing the parameter.

nodes.name: Polynomial running time
nodes.statement: The strict polynomial kernelization keeps the instances small, hence the whole process runs in polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel keeps instances small, so the process is polynomial.

nodes.name: Parameter-Non-Increasing Reduction
nodes.statement: Given two parameterized problems~$L$ with parameter~$k$ and~$L'$ with parameter~$k'$, a \emph{parameter-non-increasing reduction} from~$L$ to~$L'$ is an algorithm that maps each instance $(x,k)$ of $L$ to an equivalent instance~$(x',k')$ of~$L'$ in time polynomial in $|x|+k$ such that $k'\leq k$.

nodes.name: Diminishability transfers under two-way parameter-non-increasing reductions
nodes.statement: Let~$L_1$ and~$L_2$ be two parameterized problems such that there are parameter-non-increasing reductions from~$L_1$ to~$L_2$ and from~$L_2$ to~$L_1$. Then we have that~$L_1$ is diminishable if and only if~$L_2$ is diminishable.
assumptions: Let~$L_1$ and~$L_2$ be two parameterized problems such that there are parameter-non-increasing reductions from~$L_1$ to~$L_2$ and from~$L_2$ to~$L_1$.
conclusions: $L_1$ is diminishable if and only if~$L_2$ is diminishable
nodes.label: lem:dimreduction

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Let~$L_1$ with parameter~$k_1$ and~$L_2$ with parameter~$k_2$ be two parameterized problems. Let~$\mathcal{A}_1$ and $\mathcal{A}_2$ be parameter-non-increasing reductions from~$L_1$ to~$L_2$ and from~$L_2$ to~$L_1$, respectively. Let~$\mathcal{D}_2$ be a parameter diminisher for~$L_2$. Let $(x_1,k_1)$ be an arbitrary instance of~$L_1$. Apply $\mathcal{A}_1$ to $(x_1,k_1)$ to obtain the instance $(x_2,k_2)$ of~$L_2$ with $k_2\leq k_1$. Next, apply $\mathcal{D}_2$ to~$(x_2,k_2)$ to obtain the instance $(x_2',k_2')$ of~$L_2$ with $k_2'<k_2$. Finally, apply $\mathcal{A}_2$ to $(x_2',k_2')$ to obtain the instance~$(x_1',k_1')$ of~$L_1$ with $k_1'\leq k_2'$. As $k_1'\leq k_2'<k_2 \leq k_1$, the above combination of $\mathcal{A}_1$, $\mathcal{D}_2$, and~$\mathcal{A}_2$ forms a parameter diminisher for~$L_1$. To get the reverse direction, exchange the roles of~$L_1$ and~$L_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose reduction, diminisher of $L_2$, and back-reduction to diminish $L_1$; symmetric for the converse.

nodes.name: Fix problems, reductions and diminisher
nodes.statement:
Let~$L_1$ with parameter~$k_1$ and~$L_2$ with parameter~$k_2$ be two parameterized problems.

    Let~$\mathcal{A}_1$ and $\mathcal{A}_2$ be parameter-non-increasing reductions from~$L_1$ to~$L_2$ and from~$L_2$ to~$L_1$, respectively.
    Let~$\mathcal{D}_2$ be a parameter diminisher for~$L_2$. 
    Let $(x_1,k_1)$ be an arbitrary instance of~$L_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce reductions $\mathcal{A}_1,\mathcal{A}_2$, diminisher $\mathcal{D}_2$ and an instance.

nodes.name: Chain the three algorithms
nodes.statement:
Apply $\mathcal{A}_1$ to $(x_1,k_1)$ to obtain the instance $(x_2,k_2)$ of~$L_2$ with $k_2\leq k_1$.
    Next, apply $\mathcal{D}_2$ to~$(x_2,k_2)$ to obtain the instance $(x_2',k_2')$ of~$L_2$ with $k_2'<k_2$.
    Finally, apply $\mathcal{A}_2$ to $(x_2',k_2')$ to obtain the instance~$(x_1',k_1')$ of~$L_1$ with $k_1'\leq k_2'$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\mathcal{A}_1$, then $\mathcal{D}_2$, then $\mathcal{A}_2$.

nodes.name: Parameter strictly decreases
nodes.statement:
As $k_1'\leq k_2'<k_2 \leq k_1$, the above combination of $\mathcal{A}_1$, $\mathcal{D}_2$, and~$\mathcal{A}_2$ forms a parameter diminisher for~$L_1$.
    To get the reverse direction, exchange the roles of~$L_1$ and~$L_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain of inequalities gives a diminisher for $L_1$; swap roles for the converse.

nodes.name: Parameter-Decreasing Branching Rule
nodes.statement: A \emph{parameter-decreasing branching rule} for a parameterized problem $L$ is a polynomial-time algorithm that on input $(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ outputs a sequence of instances $(y_1,k'),\ldots,(y_t,k') \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ such that~$(x,k) \in L \iff (y_i,k') \in L$ for some $i \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$ and $k' < k$.
also_stated_at: Roughly speaking, in a \emph{parameter-decreasing branching rule} one reduces the problem instance to several problem instances with smaller parameters such that at least one of these new instances is a yes-instance if and only if the original instance is a yes-instance.
nodes.statement_short: Outputs instances with smaller parameter, one of which is yes iff the input is.
nodes.label: def:branching

nodes.name: Strict Composition
nodes.statement: A \emph{strict composition} for a parameterized problem $L$ is an algorithm that receives as input $t$ instances $(x_1,k),\ldots,(x_t,k)\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$, and outputs in polynomial~time a single instance $(y,k')\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{inparaenum}[(i)] \item $(y,k') \in L \iff (x_i,k) \in L$ for some $i \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$ and \item $k' \leq k + c$ for some constant $c$. \end{inparaenum}
nodes.statement_short: Combines $t$ instances into one OR-equivalent instance with parameter at most $k+c$.
nodes.label: def:compostion

nodes.name: Branching rule plus strict composition gives a diminisher
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem. If $L$ admits a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition, then it is diminishable.
assumptions: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem.
$L$ admits a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition
nodes.label: lem:branchcomp

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Let $(x, k)$ be an instance of a parameterized problem $L$ and $c$ be the constant associated with a strict composition for~$L$. We recursively apply the parameter-decreasing branching rule for~$L$ $c+1$ times to produce $t^{c+1}$ instances $(x_i,k^*)$ with $k^* < k-c$, since every time the parameter is decreased at least by one. The strict composition, receiving $t^{c+1}$ instances, produces an instance~$(y, k')$ with~$k'\leq k^*+c<k$ of $L$ which is a yes-instance if and only if $(x, k)$ is a yes-instance. Hence, the whole procedure is a parameter diminisher for~$L$.
nodes.statement_short: Branch $c+1$ times to drop the parameter below $k-c$, then strictly compose.

nodes.name: Branch c+1 times
nodes.statement:
Let $(x, k)$ be an instance of a parameterized problem $L$ and $c$ be the constant associated with a strict composition for~$L$. 
We recursively apply the parameter-decreasing branching rule for~$L$ $c+1$ times to produce $t^{c+1}$ instances $(x_i,k^*)$ with $k^* < k-c$, since every time the parameter is decreased at least by one.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the branching rule $c+1$ times so parameter drops below $k-c$.

nodes.name: Compose
nodes.statement: The strict composition, receiving $t^{c+1}$ instances, produces an instance~$(y, k')$ with~$k'\leq k^*+c<k$ of $L$ which is a yes-instance if and only if $(x, k)$ is a yes-instance.
nodes.statement_short: Strict composition yields an equivalent instance with $k'<k$.

nodes.name: Conclude diminisher
nodes.statement: Hence, the whole procedure is a parameter diminisher for~$L$.
nodes.statement_short: The procedure is a parameter diminisher.

nodes.name: Lemma 2 with AND-equivalence
nodes.statement: We remark that \Cref{lem:branchcomp} also holds if we require in both \Cref{def:compostion}(i) and \Cref{def:branching} that the equivalence hold for all $i \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$.

nodes.name: Parameter diminisher for Rooted Path
nodes.statement:
As an example application of \Cref{lem:branchcomp} above, we consider the parameter diminisher for the \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} problem due to Chen~\emph{et al.}~\cite{chen2011lower}. 
In this problem we are given an undirected graph~$G=(V,E)$, a distinguished vertex~$r \in V$, and an integer $k$, and our goal is to determine whether there exists a simple path in $G$ of length $k$ that starts at~$r$. 
Let $v_1,\ldots,v_t$ be the neighbors of~$r$ in $G$. 
The parameter-decreasing branching rule for \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} constructs from $(G,r,k)$ the set of instances~$(G-r,v_1,k-1),\ldots,(G-r,v_t,k-1)$. 
A strict composition for \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} takes as input the instances $(G_1,r_1,k),\ldots,(G_t,r_t,k)$ and constructs the instance~$(G',r,k+1)$, where~$G'$ is the graph obtained by taking the disjoint union of all $G_i$s and making all their roots adjacent to a new root vertex $r$. 
Combining these two algorithms gives the parameter diminisher for \pprob{Rooted Path}{k}.
nodes.statement_short: Branch on root neighbours in $G-r$, compose by joining roots to a new root; yields a diminisher for Rooted Path.

nodes.name: Non-Uniform Strict Kernel
nodes.statement: A non-uniform strict kernelization for a parameterized problem $L$ is a \emph{non-uniform} polynomial-time algorithm that on input instance~$(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ outputs an instance~$(x',k')\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$, the \emph{strict kernel}, satisfying: \begin{inparaenum}[(i)] \item $(x, k) \in L \iff (x', k') \in L$, \item $|x'| \le f(k)$, for some function $f$, and \item $k' \le k + c$, for some constant $c$. \end{inparaenum} We say that $L$ admits a non-uniform strict \emph{polynomial} kernelization if $f(k)\in k^{O(1)}$.
nodes.label: def:strictPK

nodes.name: Diminisher plus non-uniform strict polynomial kernel implies NP in P/poly
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \textnormal{NP}{}-hard and we have that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \textnormal{P}{}/\textnormal{poly}$, for some constant $c$. If $L$ is diminishable and admits a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel, then $\textnormal{NP} \subseteq \textnormal{P}/\textnormal{poly}$.
assumptions: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \textnormal{NP}{}-hard
$\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \textnormal{P}{}/\textnormal{poly}$, for some constant $c$
$L$ is diminishable and admits a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel
nodes.statement_short: Non-uniform analogue of Theorem 2: conclusion NP in P/poly.
nodes.label: prop:non-uniform

nodes.name: Karp-Lipton collapse
nodes.statement: We remark that if $\textnormal{NP} \subseteq \textnormal{P}/\textnormal{poly}$, then the Polynomial Hierarchy collapses to its second level~\cite{karp1982turing} (recall that $\textnormal{NP}{}\subseteq\textnormal{\textnormal{coNP}{}$/$poly}{}${} implies a collapse in the Polynomial Hierarchy to its third level).
assumptions: $\textnormal{NP} \subseteq \textnormal{P}/\textnormal{poly}$
conclusions: the Polynomial Hierarchy collapses to its second level

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem whose unparameterized version is \textnormal{NP}{}-hard and it holds that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \textnormal{P}{}/\textnormal{poly}$, for a constant $c\geq 1$. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a parameter diminisher for $L$ with constant $c_d\geq 1$ and let $\mathcal{A}$ be a non-uniform strict polynomial kernelization for~$L$ with constant~$c_a>1$. {}We show that we can solve any instance $(x,k)$ of $L$, with $k$ being the parameter, in non-uniform polynomial time. {} Let $(x,k)$ be an instance of $L$. Apply $\mathcal{D}$ on $(x,k)$ exactly $c_r:=\lceil (c_a+1)/c_d\rceil$~times to obtain an equivalent instance $\mathcal{D}^{c_r}(x,k)=(x',k')$ with $k'\leq k-c_d \cdot c_r< k-c_a$. Observe that the size of~$|(x', k)|$ is still polynomial in $|(x, k)|$ as $c_r$ is a constant. Next, apply $\mathcal{A}$ on $(x',k')$ to obtain an equivalent instance $(x'',k'')$ with $|(x'', k'')|\leq k'^{c'}$, $c'\geq 1$, and $k''\leq k' + c_a <k$; we explain how to get the advice for $\mathcal{A}$ in the second half of the proof. Repeating the described procedure at most~$k$ times produces an instance $(y,1)$ of $L$, solvable in non-uniform polynomial time. In the remainder of the proof, we explain how we obtain the advices for the applications of the non-uniform strict polynomial kernelization. Given any instance size $n$, we claim that for all instances $(x, k) \in L$ with $|(x, k)| = n$, we can upper-bound the sizes of all instances $(x^*, k^*)$ for which a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel needs to be computed in the above described procedure by a polynomial in $n$. Let the running time of the diminisher~$\mathcal{D}$ be $O(n^{c''})$. It follows that~$|(x',k')| \le c_O\cdot n^{c''\cdot c_r}$, where~$(x',k')=\mathcal{D}^{c_r}(x,k)$ and~$c_O$ is the constant hidden in the $O$-notation. Furthermore, we have that the size of all subsequent instances the diminisher sequence $\mathcal{D}^{c_r}$ is applied to is smaller than~$k^{c'}$. Thus, the sizes of all instances $(x^*, k^*)$ for which a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel needs to be computed can be upper-bounded by $c_O\cdot n^{c' \cdot c''\cdot c_r}$. A list containing all advices for all instance sizes smaller or equal to this bound has polynomial length, since all advices have polynomial length. Hence, the overall procedure can take that list as an advice and use it as a look-up table for the advices needed to apply the non-uniform strict polynomial kernels.
nodes.statement_short: Alternate diminisher and non-uniform strict kernel as in Theorem 2. Key step: instance sizes stay polynomial, so all advice strings fit in a polynomial look-up table.

nodes.name: Fix problem, diminisher and kernel
nodes.statement:
Let $L$ be a parameterized problem whose unparameterized version is \textnormal{NP}{}-hard and it holds that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \textnormal{P}{}/\textnormal{poly}$, for a constant $c\geq 1$. 

 Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a parameter diminisher for $L$ with constant $c_d\geq 1$ and let $\mathcal{A}$ be a non-uniform strict polynomial kernelization for~$L$ with constant~$c_a>1$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $L$, diminisher $\mathcal{D}$ and non-uniform kernel $\mathcal{A}$.

nodes.name: Solve in non-uniform polynomial time
nodes.statement:
{}We show that we can solve any instance $(x,k)$ of $L$, with $k$ being the parameter, in non-uniform polynomial time. {}
 Let $(x,k)$ be an instance of $L$.
 Apply $\mathcal{D}$ on $(x,k)$ exactly $c_r:=\lceil (c_a+1)/c_d\rceil$~times to obtain an equivalent instance $\mathcal{D}^{c_r}(x,k)=(x',k')$ with $k'\leq k-c_d \cdot c_r< k-c_a$.
 Observe that the size of~$|(x', k)|$ is still polynomial in $|(x, k)|$ as $c_r$ is a constant.
 Next, apply $\mathcal{A}$ on $(x',k')$ to obtain an equivalent instance $(x'',k'')$ with $|(x'', k'')|\leq k'^{c'}$, $c'\geq 1$, and $k''\leq k' + c_a <k$; we explain how to get the advice for $\mathcal{A}$ in the second half of the proof.
 Repeating the described procedure at most~$k$ times produces an instance $(y,1)$ of $L$, solvable in non-uniform polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: every instance is solvable in non-uniform polynomial time.

nodes.name: Diminish
nodes.statement:
Let $(x,k)$ be an instance of $L$.
 Apply $\mathcal{D}$ on $(x,k)$ exactly $c_r:=\lceil (c_a+1)/c_d\rceil$~times to obtain an equivalent instance $\mathcal{D}^{c_r}(x,k)=(x',k')$ with $k'\leq k-c_d \cdot c_r< k-c_a$.
 Observe that the size of~$|(x', k)|$ is still polynomial in $|(x, k)|$ as $c_r$ is a constant.

nodes.name: Kernelize
nodes.statement: Next, apply $\mathcal{A}$ on $(x',k')$ to obtain an equivalent instance $(x'',k'')$ with $|(x'', k'')|\leq k'^{c'}$, $c'\geq 1$, and $k''\leq k' + c_a <k$; we explain how to get the advice for $\mathcal{A}$ in the second half of the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the kernel; parameter drops below $k$.

nodes.name: Repeat
nodes.statement: Repeating the described procedure at most~$k$ times produces an instance $(y,1)$ of $L$, solvable in non-uniform polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: At most $k$ repetitions give $(y,1)$, solvable.

nodes.name: Advice construction
nodes.statement: In the remainder of the proof, we explain how we obtain the advices for the applications of the non-uniform strict polynomial kernelization.
nodes.statement_short: Explain how to obtain advice.

nodes.name: Instance sizes are polynomial
nodes.statement:
Given any instance size $n$, we claim that for all instances $(x, k) \in L$ with $|(x, k)| = n$, we can upper-bound the sizes of all instances $(x^*, k^*)$ for which a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel needs to be computed in the above described procedure by a polynomial in $n$. 
Let the running time of the diminisher~$\mathcal{D}$ be $O(n^{c''})$.
It follows that~$|(x',k')| \le c_O\cdot n^{c''\cdot c_r}$, where~$(x',k')=\mathcal{D}^{c_r}(x,k)$ and~$c_O$ is the constant hidden in the $O$-notation. 
Furthermore, we have that the size of all subsequent instances the diminisher sequence $\mathcal{D}^{c_r}$ is applied to is smaller than~$k^{c'}$. 
Thus, the sizes of all instances $(x^*, k^*)$ for which a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel needs to be computed can be upper-bounded by $c_O\cdot n^{c' \cdot c''\cdot c_r}$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: all kernelized instances have size polynomial in $n$.

nodes.name: Size after diminishing
nodes.statement:
Let the running time of the diminisher~$\mathcal{D}$ be $O(n^{c''})$.
It follows that~$|(x',k')| \le c_O\cdot n^{c''\cdot c_r}$, where~$(x',k')=\mathcal{D}^{c_r}(x,k)$ and~$c_O$ is the constant hidden in the $O$-notation.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|(x',k')|$ by $c_O n^{c''c_r}$.

nodes.name: Subsequent sizes
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we have that the size of all subsequent instances the diminisher sequence $\mathcal{D}^{c_r}$ is applied to is smaller than~$k^{c'}$.
nodes.statement_short: Later instances are smaller than $k^{c'}$.

nodes.name: Overall bound
nodes.statement: Thus, the sizes of all instances $(x^*, k^*)$ for which a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel needs to be computed can be upper-bounded by $c_O\cdot n^{c' \cdot c''\cdot c_r}$.
nodes.statement_short: All sizes bounded by $c_O n^{c'c''c_r}$.

nodes.name: Advice table
nodes.statement:
A list containing all advices for all instance sizes smaller or equal to this bound has polynomial length, since all advices have polynomial length. 
Hence, the overall procedure can take that list as an advice and use it as a look-up table for the advices needed to apply the non-uniform strict polynomial kernels.
nodes.statement_short: All advice fits in a polynomial-length look-up table.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: In this section we prove Theorem~\ref{thm:main} based on several propositions to follow.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the diminishers of the following propositions with Theorem 2.

nodes.name: Treewidth, bandwidth, cutwidth symbols
nodes.statement: Other parameterizations include treewidth~$\mathrm{tw}=\mathrm{tw}(G)$, bandwidth $\mathrm{bw}=\mathrm{bw}(G)$, and the cutwidth $\mathrm{cw}=\mathrm{cw}(G)$ of the input graph.

nodes.name: Cutwidth
nodes.statement: A graph~$G=(V,E)$ has \emph{cutwidth} at most~$k$ if and only if there exists a linear ordering (layout) $\pi: V \to \{1,\ldots,|V|\}$ of~$G$ where for each real number $1<\alpha<|V|$ we have that for the \emph{cut} at $\alpha$, defined as~$E_{\pi,\alpha}:=\{ \{u,v\} \in E: \pi(u) < \alpha < \pi(v)\}$, it holds that~$|E_{\pi,\alpha}| \leq k$.
nodes.statement_short: Cutwidth at most $k$: some linear layout has every cut $E_{\pi,\alpha}$ of size at most $k$.

nodes.name: Clique parameterized by cutwidth is diminishable
nodes.statement: \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{cw}} is diminishable.
nodes.label: lem:cliquecw

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Let $(G=(V, E), \mathrm{cw}(G), k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{cw}}. The following is a parameter-decreasing branching rule for $(G=(V, E),\mathrm{cw}(G),k)$: For each $v \in V$, let $G_v$ denote the subgraph of~$G$ induced by the open neighborhood of $v$, that is, $G_v=G[N(v)]$. It is not difficult to see that~$G$ has a clique of size $k$ if and only if some $G_v$ has a clique of size $k-1$. We next argue that $\mathrm{cw}(G_v) < \mathrm{cw}(G)$ for all $v \in V$. Consider an optimal linear ordering of~$G$, and for any vertex~$v \in V$, consider the ordering restricted to the closed neighborhood of~$v$ in the optimal ordering. By removing~$v$, we remove at least one edge in any cut of the linear ordering, giving us a linear ordering of $G_v$ which has cutwidth smaller than the optimal ordering for $G$. Hence, $\mathrm{cw}(G_v) < \mathrm{cw}(G)$ for each~$v \in V$, and the above algorithm is indeed a parameter-decreasing branching rule for \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{cw}}. For the composition step we take the disjoint union of all graphs. Since a graph has a clique of size $k$ if and only if one of its connected components has a clique of size $k$, and since the cutwidth of a graph $G$ equals the maximum cutwidth of its connected components, this is a strict composition for \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{cw}}. Applying \Cref{lem:branchcomp}, this completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Branch on open neighbourhoods $G[N(v)]$ (cutwidth drops), compose by disjoint union, apply Lemma 2.

nodes.name: Branching rule
nodes.statement:
Let $(G=(V, E), \mathrm{cw}(G), k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{cw}}. 
The following is a parameter-decreasing branching rule for $(G=(V, E),\mathrm{cw}(G),k)$: 
For each $v \in V$, let $G_v$ denote the subgraph of~$G$ induced by the open neighborhood of $v$, that is, $G_v=G[N(v)]$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $G_v=G[N(v)]$ for each vertex.

nodes.name: Clique equivalence
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to see that~$G$ has a clique of size $k$ if and only if some $G_v$ has a clique of size $k-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Clique of size $k$ in $G$ iff some $G_v$ has one of size $k-1$.

nodes.name: Restrict optimal ordering
nodes.statement:
We next argue that $\mathrm{cw}(G_v) < \mathrm{cw}(G)$ for all $v \in V$. 
Consider an optimal linear ordering of~$G$, and for any vertex~$v \in V$, consider the ordering restricted to the closed neighborhood of~$v$ in the optimal ordering.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict an optimal layout to the closed neighbourhood of $v$.

nodes.name: Cutwidth decreases
nodes.statement:
By removing~$v$, we remove at least one edge in any cut of the linear ordering, giving us a linear ordering of $G_v$ which has cutwidth smaller than the optimal ordering for $G$. 
Hence, $\mathrm{cw}(G_v) < \mathrm{cw}(G)$ for each~$v \in V$, and the above algorithm is indeed a parameter-decreasing branching rule for \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{cw}}.
nodes.statement_short: Removing $v$ cuts at least one edge per cut, so $\mathrm{cw}(G_v)<\mathrm{cw}(G)$.

nodes.name: Disjoint union composition
nodes.statement:
For the composition step we take the disjoint union of all graphs. Since a graph has a clique of size $k$ if and only if one of its connected components has a clique of size $k$, and since the cutwidth of a graph $G$ equals the maximum cutwidth of its connected components, this is a strict composition for \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{cw}}. 
Applying \Cref{lem:branchcomp}, this completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Disjoint union is a strict composition; Lemma 2 concludes.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement:
Note that the above procedure is also a parameter diminisher for parameters $\Delta$, $\mathrm{tw}$, $\mathrm{bw}$, and $k$. 
Leaving the \W{1}-complete \pprob{Clique}{k} problem aside, we get the following corollary.
nodes.statement_short: The Clique diminisher also decreases $\Delta$, tw and bw.

nodes.name: Clique parameterized by degree, treewidth, bandwidth is diminishable
nodes.statement: \pprob{Clique}{\Delta}, \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{tw}}, and \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{bw}} are diminishable.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2
nodes.statement: It is easy to show that the parameter diminisher presented for \prob{Clique} can be adapted to the \textsc{Biclique} problem: Given an undirected bipartite graph $G=(A \uplus B, E)$ and an integer $k$, find~$k$ vertices $a_1,\ldots,a_k \in A$ and $b_1,\ldots,b_k\in B$ such that $\{a_i,b_j\} \in E$ for all $1 \leq i , j \leq k$. Thus, we have:
nodes.statement_short: Adapt the Clique diminisher to Biclique.

nodes.name: Biclique parameterized by degree and width measures is diminishable
nodes.statement: \pprob{Biclique}{\Delta}, \pprob{Biclique}{\mathrm{tw}}, \pprob{Biclique}{\mathrm{bw}}, and \pprob{Biclique}{\mathrm{cw}} are diminishable.
nodes.label: lem:bicliquecw

nodes.name: Steiner Tree
nodes.statement: We next consider an \textnormal{NP}-complete variant of the well-known \textsc{Steiner Tree} problem: given an undirected graph $G=(V=N\uplus T,E)$ ($T$ is called the terminal set) and a positive integer~$k$, decide whether there is a subgraph~$H\subseteq G$ with at most $k+|T|$ vertices such that~$H$ is a tree containing all vertices in~$T$.
nodes.statement_short: Find a tree with at most $k+|T|$ vertices spanning terminal set $T$.

nodes.name: Terminal Steiner Tree is FPT
nodes.statement: \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|} is fixed parameter tractable.
conclusions: \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|} is fixed parameter tractable.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: We give an FPT-reduction from \pprob{TST}{k+|T|} to \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|}. As \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|} is fixed-parameter tractable~\cite{DreyfusW71}, the claim follows. Let $(G=(N\uplus T,E),k)$ be an instance of \pprob{TST}{k+|T|}. We construct an equivalent instance~$(G'=(N'\uplus T,E'),k')$ of \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|} as follows. Let $G'$ be initially a copy of~$G$. For each~$t\in T$, apply the following. For each edge~$\{v,t\}\in E$, remove~$\{v,t\}$ from~$G'$ and add a path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ to~$G'$ with endpoints~$v$ and~$t$. Set~$k'=|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+k$. This finishes the reduction. Clearly, the construction can be done in FPT-time. We show that $(G=(N\uplus T,E),k)$ is a yes-instance of \pprob{TST}{k+|T|} if and only if $(G'=(N'\uplus T,E'),k')$ is a yes-instance of \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|}. Let~$H$ be a terminal Steiner tree in~$G$ with $\ell\leq k+|T|$ vertices. We construct a Steiner tree~$H'$ in~$G'$ from~$H$ with $\ell'\leq k'+|T|$ vertices as follows. Recall that each~$t\in T$ has exactly one neighbor~$v_t$ in~$H$. Hence, obtain~$H'$ by replacing for each~$t\in T$ the edge~$\{v_t,t\}\in E(H)$ by the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$. It is not difficult to see~$H'$ is a Steiner tree in~$G'$. Moreover, $\ell'=|V(H')|=|V(H)|+|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)\leq k+|T|+|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)=k'+|T|$. Conversely, let~$H'$ be a minimum Steiner tree in~$G'$ with $\ell'\leq k'+|T|$ vertices. We state some first observations on~$H'$. Observe that no inner vertex of the paths added in the construction step from~$G$ to~$G'$ is a leaf of~$H'$ (as otherwise~$H'$ is not minimum). Moreover, as~$H'$ contains each~$t\in T$,~$H'$ contains a path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ for each~$t\in T$. Suppose that there is a terminal~$t\in T$ such that~$t$ is not a leaf in~$H'$. Then~$H'$ contains at least~$|T|+(|T|+1)\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)=|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+2(k+|T|)-1=k'+(k+|T|)-1>k'+|T|$, yielding a contradiction. Hence, each terminal~$t\in T$ forms a leaf in~$H'$. We show how to obtain a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ in~$G$ from~$H'$ with at most~$k+|T|$ vertices. As each terminal~$t\in T$ forms a leaf in~$H'$, there is exactly one neighbor~$v_t\in N_G(t)$ such that~$H'$ contains the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$. Replace for each~$t\in T$ the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$ in~$H'$ by the edge~$\{v_t,t\}\in E$ to obtain~$H$ from~$H'$. Note that~$H$ is a terminal Steiner tree. Moreover, $|V(H)|=|V(H')|-|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)\leq |T|+|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+k-|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)=k+|T|$.
nodes.statement_short: FPT reduction to Steiner Tree by subdividing terminal edges into long paths. Key step: a minimum Steiner tree must use terminals as leaves, else it is too large.

nodes.name: Reduce to Steiner Tree
nodes.statement: We give an FPT-reduction from \pprob{TST}{k+|T|} to \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|}. As \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|} is fixed-parameter tractable~\cite{DreyfusW71}, the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce TST to the FPT problem Steiner Tree.

nodes.name: Construction
nodes.statement:
Let $(G=(N\uplus T,E),k)$ be an instance of \pprob{TST}{k+|T|}.
We construct an equivalent instance~$(G'=(N'\uplus T,E'),k')$ of \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|} as follows.
Let $G'$ be initially a copy of~$G$.
For each~$t\in T$, apply the following.
For each edge~$\{v,t\}\in E$, remove~$\{v,t\}$ from~$G'$ and add a path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ to~$G'$ with endpoints~$v$ and~$t$.
Set~$k'=|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+k$.
This finishes the reduction.
Clearly, the construction can be done in FPT-time.
nodes.statement_short: Replace terminal edges by paths of length $2(k+|T|)$ and set $k'$.

nodes.name: Equivalence to show
nodes.statement: We show that $(G=(N\uplus T,E),k)$ is a yes-instance of \pprob{TST}{k+|T|} if and only if $(G'=(N'\uplus T,E'),k')$ is a yes-instance of \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|}.
nodes.statement_short: State the equivalence of instances.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement:
Let~$H$ be a terminal Steiner tree in~$G$ with $\ell\leq k+|T|$ vertices.
We construct a Steiner tree~$H'$ in~$G'$ from~$H$ with $\ell'\leq k'+|T|$ vertices as follows.
Recall that each~$t\in T$ has exactly one neighbor~$v_t$ in~$H$.
Hence, obtain~$H'$ by replacing for each~$t\in T$ the edge~$\{v_t,t\}\in E(H)$ by the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$.
It is not difficult to see~$H'$ is a Steiner tree in~$G'$.
Moreover, $\ell'=|V(H')|=|V(H)|+|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)\leq k+|T|+|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)=k'+|T|$.
nodes.statement_short: Subdivide terminal edges of $H$ to get a small Steiner tree.

nodes.name: Backward direction
nodes.statement:
Conversely, let~$H'$ be a minimum Steiner tree in~$G'$ with $\ell'\leq k'+|T|$ vertices.
We state some first observations on~$H'$.
Observe that no inner vertex of the paths added in the construction step from~$G$ to~$G'$ is a leaf of~$H'$ (as otherwise~$H'$ is not minimum).
Moreover, as~$H'$ contains each~$t\in T$,~$H'$ contains a path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ for each~$t\in T$.
Suppose that there is a terminal~$t\in T$ such that~$t$ is not a leaf in~$H'$.
Then~$H'$ contains at least~$|T|+(|T|+1)\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)=|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+2(k+|T|)-1=k'+(k+|T|)-1>k'+|T|$, yielding a contradiction.
Hence, each terminal~$t\in T$ forms a leaf in~$H'$.
We show how to obtain a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ in~$G$ from~$H'$ with at most~$k+|T|$ vertices.
As each terminal~$t\in T$ forms a leaf in~$H'$, there is exactly one neighbor~$v_t\in N_G(t)$ such that~$H'$ contains the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$.
Replace for each~$t\in T$ the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$ in~$H'$ by the edge~$\{v_t,t\}\in E$ to obtain~$H$ from~$H'$.
Note that~$H$ is a terminal Steiner tree.
Moreover, $|V(H)|=|V(H')|-|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)\leq |T|+|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+k-|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)=k+|T|$.
nodes.statement_short: Show terminals are leaves of $H'$ and contract paths.

nodes.name: Observations on H'
nodes.statement:
Conversely, let~$H'$ be a minimum Steiner tree in~$G'$ with $\ell'\leq k'+|T|$ vertices.
We state some first observations on~$H'$.
Observe that no inner vertex of the paths added in the construction step from~$G$ to~$G'$ is a leaf of~$H'$ (as otherwise~$H'$ is not minimum).
Moreover, as~$H'$ contains each~$t\in T$,~$H'$ contains a path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ for each~$t\in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Inner path vertices are not leaves; $H'$ contains a long path per terminal.

nodes.name: Terminals are leaves
nodes.statement:
Suppose that there is a terminal~$t\in T$ such that~$t$ is not a leaf in~$H'$.
Then~$H'$ contains at least~$|T|+(|T|+1)\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)=|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+2(k+|T|)-1=k'+(k+|T|)-1>k'+|T|$, yielding a contradiction.
Hence, each terminal~$t\in T$ forms a leaf in~$H'$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-leaf terminal makes $H'$ too large.

nodes.name: Contract paths
nodes.statement:
We show how to obtain a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ in~$G$ from~$H'$ with at most~$k+|T|$ vertices.
As each terminal~$t\in T$ forms a leaf in~$H'$, there is exactly one neighbor~$v_t\in N_G(t)$ such that~$H'$ contains the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$.
Replace for each~$t\in T$ the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$ in~$H'$ by the edge~$\{v_t,t\}\in E$ to obtain~$H$ from~$H'$.
Note that~$H$ is a terminal Steiner tree.
Moreover, $|V(H)|=|V(H')|-|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)\leq |T|+|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+k-|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)=k+|T|$.
nodes.statement_short: Contract paths back to edges to get a terminal Steiner tree of size $k+|T|$.

nodes.name: No polynomial kernel for TST under NP not in coNP/poly
nodes.statement:
We can reduce \pprob{Steiner tree}{k+|T|} to \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|} by adding to each terminal a pendant leaf.

Set the terminal set in TST to the set of added leaf vertices, and ask for a terminal Steiner tree of size $k'=k+|T|$.
This is a polynomial parameter transformation, and hence refutes the existence of a polynomial problem kernel~\cite{DLS14} for TST under $\textnormal{NP}{}\nsubseteq\textnormal{\textnormal{coNP}{}$/$poly}{}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pendant leaves give a polynomial parameter transformation from Steiner Tree, excluding polynomial kernels for TST.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: We present a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition for \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|}. Together with~\Cref{lem:branchcomp}, the claim then follows. Let~$(G=(N\uplus T,E), k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|} (we can assume that $G$ has a connected component containing~$T$). We make several assumptions first. We can assume that~$|T|\geq 3$ (otherwise a shortest path is the optimal solution) and additionally that for all terminals $t\in T$ it holds that~$N_G(t)\not\subseteq T$ (as otherwise the instance is a no-instance). Moreover, we can assume that there is no vertex~$v\in N$ such that $T\subseteq N_G(v)$, as otherwise we immediately output whether $k\geq 1$. Select a terminal $t^*\in T$, and let $v_1,\ldots,v_d$ denote the neighbors of~$t^*$ in~$G-(T\setminus\{t^*\})$. We create $d$ instances $(G_1,k-1),\ldots,(G_d,k-1)$ as follows. Define~$G_i$, $i\in[d]$, by $G_i:=G-v_i$. Turn the vertices in~$N_G(v_i)$ in~$G_i$ into a clique, that is, for each distinct vertices $v,w\in N_G(v_i)$ add the edge~$\{v,w\}$ if not yet present. This finishes the construction of~$G_i$. It is not hard to see that the construction can be done in polynomial time. We show that~$G$ has a terminal Steiner tree of size~$k+|T|$ if and only if there is an~$i\in[d]$ such that~$G_i$ admits a terminal Steiner tree of size~$k-1+|T|$. Suppose that~$G$ has a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ of size~$k+|T|$. As~$t^*$ is a leaf in~$H$, there is exactly one neighbor $v_i$, $i\in[d]$, being the neighbor of~$t^*$ in~$H$. Let~$w$ be a neighbor of~$v_i$ in~$H-T$ and let $A:=N_H(v_i)$ (note that~$t^*\in A$). Then~$H_i$ forms a terminal Steiner tree in~$G_i$, where~$H_i$ is the tree obtained from~$H$ by deleting~$v_i$ and connecting~$w$ with all vertices in~$A$. Moreover, $H_i$ is of size~$k-1+|T|$. Conversely, let $G_i$ admit a terminal Steiner tree~$H_i$ of size~$k-1+|T|$. As~$t^*$ is a leaf in~$H_i$, there is exactly one vertex~$w$ being the neighbor of~$t^*$ in~$H_i$. We obtain a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ in~$G$ from~$H_i$ as follows. If every edge in~$H_i$ is also present in~$G$, then~$H:=H_i$ also forms a terminal Steiner tree in~$G$. Otherwise, there is an inclusion-wise maximal edge set~$E'\subseteq E(H_i)$ such that $E'\cap E(G)=\emptyset$. Observe that by construction, the set of endpoints of~$E'$ forms a subset of~$N_G(v_i)$. Let initially~$H$ be a copy of~$H_i$. Delete from~$H$ all edges in~$E'$, add vertex~$v_i$ to~$H$, and for each~$\{x,y\}\in E'$, add the edges~$\{x,v_i\}$ and~$\{y,v_i\}$. Note that~$H$ remains connected after this step, and the set of leaves remains unchanged. Finally, compute a minimum feedback edge set in~$H$ if necessary. Observe that since~$V(H)=V(H_i)\cup\{v_i\}$, $H$ forms a terminal Steiner tree of size~$k+|T|$ in~$G$. Next, we describe the strict composition for \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|}. Given the instances $(G_1,k),\ldots,(G_d,k)$, we create an instance $(G',k)$ as follows. Let~$G'$ be initially the disjoint union of~$G_1,\ldots,G_d$. For each $t\in T$, identify its copies in~$G_1,\ldots,G_d$, say~$t_1,\ldots,t_d$, with one vertex~$t'$ corresponding to~$t$. This finishes the construction of~$G'$. Note that for every $i,j\in[d]$, $i\neq j$, any path between a vertex in~$G_i$ and a vertex in $G_j$ contains a terminal vertex. Hence, any terminal Steiner tree in $G'$ contains non-terminal vertices only in~$G_i$ for exactly one~$i\in[d]$. It is not difficult to see that $(G',k)$ is a yes-instance if and only if one of the instances~$(G_1,k),\ldots,(G_d,k)$ is a yes-instance.
nodes.statement_short: Branch on neighbours $v_i$ of a terminal, deleting $v_i$ and turning its neighbourhood into a clique; compose by identifying terminals. Key step: rebuild a tree in $G$ from $G_i$ by re-inserting $v_i$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement: We present a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition for \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k}. The result will then follow directly from \Cref{lem:branchcomp}. Let $(G=(V,E),\mathrm{col})$ be an instance of the \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} problem. The parameter-decreasing branching rule for~$(G=(V,E),\mathrm{col})$ creates a graph $G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ for each ordered triplet $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ of vertices of~$V$ such that $v_1,v_2,v_3$ is a multicolored path in $G$. The graph~$G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ is constructed from $G$ as follows: We delete from $G$ all vertices $w\in V\setminus\{v_2,v_3\}$ with~$\mathrm{col}(w)\in\{\mathrm{col}(v_1),\mathrm{col}(v_2),\mathrm{col}(v_3)\}$. Following this, only vertices of $k-1$ colors remain, and $v_2$ and~$v_3$ are the only vertices colored $\mathrm{col}(v_2)$ and $\mathrm{col}(v_3)$, respectively. We then delete all edges incident with~$v_2$, apart from $\{v_2,v_3\}$, and relabel all colors so that the image of $\mathrm{col}$ for~$G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ is~$\{1,\ldots,k-1\}$. Clearly our parameter decreasing branching rule can be performed in polynomial time. Furthermore, the parameter decreases in each output instance. We show that the first requirement of Definition~\ref{def:branching} holds as well: Indeed, suppose that $G$ has a multicolored path~$v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k$ of length~$k$. Then $v_2,\ldots,v_k$ is a multicolored path of length~$k-1$ in~$G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ by construction. Conversely, suppose there is a multicolored path $u_2,\ldots,u_k$ of length $k-1$ in some $G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$. Then since $v_2$ is the only vertex of color $\mathrm{col}(v_2)$ in $G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$, and since $v_2$ is only adjacent to~$v_3$, it must be w.l.o.g.\ that $u_2=v_2$ and $u_3=v_3$. Therefore, since $v_1$ is adjacent to $v_2$ in $G$, and no vertices of $u_2,\ldots,u_k$ have color $\mathrm{col}(v_1)$ in $G$, the sequence of $v_1,u_2,\ldots,u_k$ forms a multicolored path of length $k$ in~$G$. The strict composition for \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} is as follows. Given a sequence of inputs~$(G_1,\mathrm{col}_1),\ldots,(G_t,\mathrm{col}_t)$, the strict composition constructs the disjoint union $G$ and the coloring function~$\mathrm{col}$ of all graphs $G_i$ and coloring functions $\mathrm{col}_i$, $1\leq i\leq t$. Clearly, $(G,\mathrm{col})$ contains a multicolored path of length $k$ if and only if there is a multicolored path of length $k$ in some~$(G_i,\mathrm{col}_i)$. The result thus follows directly from \Cref{lem:branchcomp}.
nodes.statement_short: Branch on multicolored triples $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, deleting colours so $v_2$ becomes a forced start; compose by disjoint union.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5
nodes.statement: Chen, Flum, and M\"{u}ller~\cite[Prop.~3.10]{chen2011lower} proved that if $L$ is a parameterized problem which can be solved in $2^{k^{O(1)}}|x|^{O(1)}$ time, where $k$ is the parameter and $|x|$ is the instance size, then $L(k)$ has a polynomial kernel if and only if $L(k \log |x|)$ has a polynomial kernel. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6
nodes.statement: We show that there is a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition for \pprob{Colorful Graph Motif}{k}. Let $(G=(V,E),\mathrm{col})$ be an instance of \pprob{Colorful Graph Motif}{k}. Assume there are only edges between differently colored vertices. For each~$\{v, w\} \in E$, the parameter-decreasing branching rule creates a graph $G_{\{v, w\}}$ which is a copy of~$G$ where all vertices of colors $\mathrm{col}(v)$ and $\mathrm{col}(w)$ are removed. Furthermore, a new vertex $v^\star$ is added with color $\mathrm{col}(v^\star) = \mathrm{col}(v)$ and with edges to all vertices in~$N(v)\cup N(w)$ that have not been removed. Clearly,~$G_{\{v, w\}}$ only contains vertices of $k-1$ different colors and is computable in polynomial time. Also, if $G$ contains a colorful motif~$\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_k\}$ where, without loss of generality, $\{v_1, v_2\} \in E$, then $G_{\{v_1, v_2\}}$ contains the colorful motif~$\{v^\star, v_3, \ldots, v_k\}$. Conversely, if a graph $G_{\{v, w\}}$ contains a colorful motif, then it has to contain~$v^\star$ since it is the only vertex of its color. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: The main idea behind the parameter diminisher for \pprob{Short NTM Computation}{k+|\Sigma|} is to transform the given Turing machine $M$ to a Turing machine $M'=(\Sigma,Q',q'_0,F',\delta')$ that computes the last two steps of $M$, that is step $k-1$ and step $k$, in one step. (If $k=1$, then the parameter diminisher can produce a trivial YES{}- or NO-instance.) To do that, we need to encode the letter and its position on the tape that will be read by Turing machine~$M$ in step $k$ in the states of Turing machine $M'$. Additionally, we need to use the states to count the steps in order to allow the Turing machine $M'$ to recognize when it has to compute two steps of $M$ in one step, and we need to encode the position of the tape which the head is currently looking at. Let $x\in \Sigma^*$ denote the input string, that is initially written on the tape, starting at cell $0$. Note that in $k$ steps, the head of the Turing machine can potentially only move to and read from cells $-k, -k+1, \ldots, 0, \ldots, k-1, k$, assuming the initial head position is $0$. Hence, we set $$Q' = \{q_0'\}\cup (Q\times (\Sigma\cup \{\square\})\times\{-k,\dots,k\}\times\{-k,\dots,k\}\times\{1,\dots,k-1\})\cup \{\bar{q}\}.$$ So every state different from $q_0'$ and $\bar{q}$ is a tuple consisting of five elements: the state of Turing machine $M$ it corresponds to, the letter that is on a specific position of the tape, that position, the current position of the head, and the current computation step. Every of those states is accepting, it the corresponding state of $M$ is accepting, $q_0'$ is accepting if $q_0$ is accepting, and $\bar{q}$ is not an accepting state. For every transition in $\delta$ from the initial state $q_0$ to some state $q$ we create transitions in~$\delta'$ from the new initial state $q_0'$ to all states $(q,x_i, i, m, 1)$ such that the following conditions are met. \begin{compactitem} \item $-k\leq i\leq k$, \item for $1\le i \le |x|$, $x_i$ is the $i$-th letter of input $x$, for $i=0$, $x_0$ is the letter written by $\delta$ to cell~$0$, and $\square$ otherwise, and \item $m$ is the movement of the head in the transition $\delta$, that is, $m\in\{-1, 0, 1\}$. \end{compactitem} The following stays unchanged in the transition: the letter that needs to be read by the head for the transition to be possible, the letter written to the tape, and the movement of the head. For every transition from a state $q$ to a state $q'$ in $\delta$, we create transitions from states~$(q, x, i, j, t)$ to states $(q', x', i, j', t+1)$ in $\delta'$, such that the following conditions are met. \begin{compactitem} \item $-k\leq i\leq k$, \item $x'=x$ unless we have that $i=j$, in this case the Turing machine writes symbol $y$ into cell $i$ in that transition $\delta$, and hence $x' = y$, \item $j' = j+m$, where $m$ is the movement of the head in the transition $\delta$, that is, $m\in\{-1, 0, 1\}$, and \item $1\le t \le k-3$. \end{compactitem} Again, the following stays unchanged in the transition: the letter that needs to be read by the head for the transition to be possible, the letter written to the tape, and the movement of the head. Finally, for every state $(q, x, i, j, k-2)$ we create a transition in $\delta'$ that on reading symbol $y$ goes to state $(q', x', i, j', k-1)$ without moving the head if the following conditions are met. \begin{compactitem} \item There is a transition from $q$ on reading symbol $y$ to a state $q^\star$ in $\delta$ with head movement~$m$ such that $j+m=i$, and \item there is a transition in $\delta$ that, if $M$ is in state $q^\star$ and reads $x$, goes to state $q'$. \end{compactitem} Otherwise, we create a transition in $\delta'$ that goes from state $(q, x, i, j, k-2)$ and reading symbol $y$ to state $\bar{q}$ without moving the head. No writing is necessary. Turing machine $M'$ needs to non-deterministically guess the position of the head of Turing machine $M$ in step $k-1$ and then simulates the behavior of $M$ until step $k-2$. If the guess was wrong, then $M$ will transition to $\bar{q}$, a non-accepting state. If the guess was correct, then $M'$ accepts in $k-1$ steps if and only if $M$ accepts in $k$ steps.
nodes.statement_short: Build $M'$ whose states record a guessed tape cell's letter, the head position and a step counter, so the last two steps of $M$ are done in one step.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 8
nodes.statement: The idea behind the parameter diminisher for \pprob{Short NTM Computation}{k+|Q|} is to merge the symbols on the tape at positions $-1,0,+1$ into a single new symbol. In this way we can produce a Turing machine $M'$ that computes the first two steps of the given Turing machine~$M$ with a single step. (If $k=1$, then the parameter diminisher can produce a trivial YES{}- or NO-instance.) More specifically, given a Turing machine $M=(\Sigma, Q, q_0, F, \delta)$, a word $x\in\Sigma^*$, and a positive integer $k$, we construct a Turing machine $M'=(\Sigma',Q,q_0,F,\delta')$ and a word $x'\in\Sigma'^*$ such that~$(M',x',k-1)$ is a YES{}-instance if and only if $(M,x,k)$ is a YES{}-instance. We set~$\Sigma'=\Sigma\cup\left((\Sigma\cup\{\square\})\times\Sigma^2\times\{-1,0,+1,S\}\right)$. The set $\{-1,0,+1,S\}$ encodes the position of the head of $M$ when reading a symbol at positions $-1,0,+1$, while $S$ encodes that this is the first step, and hence that we need to compute two steps of $M$ at once. The new input $x'$ is set to~$x'=(\square,x_0,x_1,S) x_2 \dots x_n$, where $x_0\dots x_n=x$. The transition relation $\delta'$ is defined as follows. On symbols in $\Sigma$ the Turing machine~$M'$ behaves like $M$, while on symbols $(\sigma_{-1},\sigma_{0},\sigma_{+1},i)$ with $i\in\{-1, 0, 1\}$, we simulate the original Turing machine $M$ on the character $\sigma_i$. If the Turing machine~$M$ moves left or right within~$\{-1,0,1\}$, then we keep the head on the same position and update the value of~$i$. If we move outside the range $\{-1,0,+1\}$, then we move the head to the left and right accordingly. Note that when the Turing machine~$M'$ returns to this symbol, then the value of $i$ will be automatically correct. Finally, on symbols $(\sigma_{-1},\sigma_{0},\sigma_{+1},S)$ we are in state $q_0$ and simulate the first two steps of the Turing machine $M$. Also, we replace $S$ according to the movement of the head. This guarantees that $M'$ will only read such a symbol in the very first step and hence computes two steps of $M$ in one step exactly once. It is not difficult to see that $M'$ accepts $x'$ in $k-1$ steps if and only if $M$ accepts $x$ in $k$ steps.
nodes.statement_short: Merge tape cells $-1,0,+1$ into one symbol so $M'$ simulates the first two steps of $M$ in one step.

nodes.name: Semi-Strict Kernel
nodes.statement: A \emph{semi-strict kernelization} for a parameterized problem~$L$~is a polynomial-time algorithm that on input instance $(x,k)\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ outputs an instance~$(x',k')\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$, the \emph{semi-strict kernel}, satisfying: \begin{inparaenum}[(i)] \item $(x, k) \in L \iff (x', k') \in L$, \item $|x'| \le f(k)$, for some function $f$, and \item $k' \le c\cdot k $, for some constant $c$. \end{inparaenum} We say that~$L$~admits a semi-strict \emph{polynomial} kernelization if $f(k)\in k^{O(1)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Like a strict kernel but the parameter may grow by a constant factor.
nodes.label: def:lessstrictPK

nodes.name: Semi-strict kernels generalize strict kernels
nodes.statement:
On the one hand, every strict kernelization with constant~$c$ is a semi-strict kernelizations with constant~$c+1$.
  On the other hand, if a parameterized problem~$L$ admits a semi-strict kernel with constant $c$, there is not necessarily a constant $c'$ such that for \emph{every} input instance $(x,k)$, the obtained parameter value~$k'$ of the output instance~$(x',k')$ is upper-bounded by $k'+c'$.
  Hence,~$L$ does not necessarily admit a strict kernelization.
  In this sense, \Cref{def:lessstrictPK} generalizes strict kernelizations.

nodes.name: Theorem 2 does not exclude semi-strict kernels
nodes.statement:
Note that \Cref{thm:diminisher} in \Cref{sec:framework} does not imply that the problems mentioned in~\Cref{thm:main} do not admit semi-strict polynomial kernelizations unless $\textnormal{P}{}=\textnormal{NP}{}${}.
Intuitively, in \Cref{thm:diminisher}, the parameter diminisher is constantly often applied to decrease the parameter, while dealing only with a constant additive blow-up of the parameter caused by the strict kernelization.
When dealing with a constant multiplicative blow-up of the parameter caused by the semi-strict kernelization, the parameter diminisher is required to be applied a non-constant number of times.
Hence, to deal with semi-strict kernelization, we introduce a stronger version of our parameter diminisher.

nodes.name: Strong Parameter Diminisher
nodes.statement: A \emph{strong parameter diminisher} for a parameterized problem $L$ is a polynomial-time algorithm that maps instances $(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ to instances~$(x', k') \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ such that $(x, k) \in L \text{ if and only if } (x', k') \in L$, and $k' \le k/c$, for some constant $c>1$.
differentia: $(x, k) \in L \text{ if and only if } (x', k') \in L$
nodes.label: def:strongdiminisher

nodes.name: Strong diminisher constant at least two
nodes.statement: To simplify arguments in the proofs, we assume without loss of generality that the constant of any strong diminisher is at least two for the remainder of this section. Consider a strong parameter diminisher $\mathcal{D}$ with constant $1<c<2$. Let $\mathcal{D}'$ be the repetition of $\mathcal{D}$ exactly $\lceil\log_c 2\rceil$~times. Then~$\mathcal{D}'$ is a strong parameter diminisher with constant $c':=c^{\lceil\log_c 2\rceil}\geq 2$.

nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \textnormal{NP}{}-hard and we have that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \textnormal{P}{}$, for some constant $c\geq 1$. If $L$ is strongly diminishable and admits a semi-strict polynomial kernel, then $\textnormal{P}{}=\textnormal{NP}{}${}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem whose unparameterized version is \textnormal{NP}{}-hard and it holds that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \textnormal{P}{}$, for a constant $c\geq 1$. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a strong parameter diminisher for $L$ with constant $c_d\geq 2$ and let $\mathcal{A}$ be a semi-strict polynomial kernelization for~$L$ with constant~$c_a>1$. {}We show that we can solve any instance $(x,k)$ of $L$, with $k$ being the parameter, in polynomial time. {} Let $(x,k)$ be an instance of $L$. Apply $\mathcal{D}$ on $(x,k)$ exactly $c_r:=\lceil\log_{c_d}(c_a+c_d)\rceil$~times to obtain an equivalent instance $\mathcal{D}^{c_r}(x,k)=(x',k')$ with $k'\leq k/c_d^{c_r}\leq k/(c_a+c_d)$. Observe that the size of~$|(x', k')|$ is still polynomial in $|(x, k)|$ as $c_r$ is a constant. Next, apply $\mathcal{A}$ on $(x',k')$ to obtain an equivalent instance $(x'',k'')$ with $|(x'', k'')|\leq k'^{c'}$, $c'\geq 1$, and $k''\leq c_a\cdot k'\leq c_a\cdot k/(c_a+c_d)<k$. Repeating the described procedure at most $k$ times produces an instance $(y,1)$ of $L$, solvable in polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the strong diminisher a constant number of times, then the semi-strict kernel; parameter shrinks each round.

nodes.name: No semi-strict polynomial kernel for Set Cover and Hitting Set
nodes.statement: Unless $\textnormal{P}{}=\textnormal{NP}{}${}, \pprob{Set Cover}{k \log n} and \pprob{Hitting Set}{k \log m} does not admit a semi-strict polynomial kernel.
assumptions: Unless $\textnormal{P}{}=\textnormal{NP}{}${}
conclusions: \pprob{Set Cover}{k \log n} and \pprob{Hitting Set}{k \log m} does not admit a semi-strict polynomial kernel.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Let $(U, \mathcal{F} = \{F_1, \ldots, F_m\}, k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Set Cover}{k\log n} and assume that~$k\geq 2$ and $n\geq 5$. If $k$ is odd, then we add a unique element to~$U$, a unique set containing only this element to~$\mathcal{F}$, and we set~$k=k+1$. Hence, we assume that~$k$~is even. The following procedure is a strong parameter diminisher for the problem parameterized by $k\log n$. Let $U' = U$ and for all~$F_i, F_j$ create $F'_{\{i, j\}} = F_i \cup F_j$. Let $\mathcal{F}' = \{F'_{\{i, j\}} \ | \ i\neq j\}$ and set $k' = k/2$. This yields the instance~$(U', \mathcal{F}', k')$ of \pprob{Set Cover}{k\log n} in polynomial time. {}In the following we {}show that $(U, \mathcal{F}, k)$ is a yes-instance if and only if $(U', \mathcal{F}', k')$ is a yes-instance{}. Furthermore, we argue that {}$k'\log n' < (k\log n)/c$ for some constant~$c>1$, where $n'=|U'|$. \toappendix { Assume that there is a set cover $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{F}$ for~$U$ of size~$k$. Let $\mathcal{C} = \{C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_k\}$ and let $\mathcal{C}' = \{C_1\cup C_2, C_3\cup C_4, \ldots, C_{k-1}\cup C_k\}$. Then clearly $\mathcal{C}'\subseteq \mathcal{F}'$ is a set cover for~$U'$ of size~$k/2$. Conversely, assume that there is a set cover $\mathcal{C}'$ for $U'$ of size $k/2$. Let $\mathcal{C}' = \{C_1', C_2', \ldots, C_{k/2}'\}$, let $C_i'=C_i\cup C_{i'}$ and let $\mathcal{C} = \{C_1, C_{1'}, C_2, C_{2'},\ldots,C_{k/2},C_{k/2'}\}$. Then clearly $\mathcal{C}\subseteq \mathcal{F}$ is a set cover for $U$ of size at most~$k$. Furthermore, we have that $m' = {m \choose 2}$. It follows that \[k'\log n' \leq \frac{k+1}{2}\log (n+1) \stackrel{k\geq 2}{\leq} \frac{3k}{4}\log (n+1) \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}k\log ((n+1)^{\sqrt{3}/2}) \stackrel{n\geq 5}{\leq} \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}k\log (n).\] Note that in the first inequality, we consider the cases of $k$ being modified to be even. It follows that for $k>2$ the parameter decreases by at least a factor of $\sqrt{3}/{2}$ and for $k=2$ the parameter diminisher produces either a trivial yes- or a trivial no-instance. } It is easy to see that a strong parameter diminisher for \pprob{Hitting Set}{k \log m} can be constructed in a similar fashion.
nodes.statement_short: Strong diminisher: pair up sets ($F_i\cup F_j$) and halve $k$; parameter $k\log n$ shrinks by factor $\sqrt3/2$.

nodes.name: Make k even
nodes.statement:
Let $(U, \mathcal{F} = \{F_1, \ldots, F_m\}, k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Set Cover}{k\log n} and assume that~$k\geq 2$ and $n\geq 5$.
  If $k$ is odd, then we add a unique element to~$U$, a unique set containing only this element to~$\mathcal{F}$, and we set~$k=k+1$.
  Hence, we assume that~$k$~is even.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $k\ge2$, $n\ge5$, and pad to make $k$ even.

nodes.name: Pair sets
nodes.statement:
The following procedure is a strong parameter diminisher for the problem parameterized by $k\log n$. 
  Let $U' = U$ and for all~$F_i, F_j$ create $F'_{\{i, j\}} = F_i \cup F_j$. Let $\mathcal{F}' = \{F'_{\{i, j\}} \ | \ i\neq j\}$ and set $k' = k/2$.
  This yields the instance~$(U', \mathcal{F}', k')$ of \pprob{Set Cover}{k\log n} in polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: Let $\mathcal{F}'$ be all pairwise unions, $k'=k/2$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: {}In the following we {}show that $(U, \mathcal{F}, k)$ is a yes-instance if and only if $(U', \mathcal{F}', k')$ is a yes-instance{}. Furthermore, we argue that {}$k'\log n' < (k\log n)/c$ for some constant~$c>1$, where $n'=|U'|$.
nodes.statement_short: Show equivalence and parameter shrinkage.

nodes.name: Forward
nodes.statement:
Assume that there is a set cover $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{F}$ for~$U$ of size~$k$. 
    Let $\mathcal{C} = \{C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_k\}$ and let $\mathcal{C}' = \{C_1\cup C_2, C_3\cup C_4, \ldots, C_{k-1}\cup C_k\}$. 
    Then clearly $\mathcal{C}'\subseteq \mathcal{F}'$ is a set cover for~$U'$ of size~$k/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Pair up the $k$ cover sets.

nodes.name: Backward and shrinkage
nodes.statement:
Conversely, assume that there is a set cover $\mathcal{C}'$ for $U'$ of size $k/2$. 
    Let $\mathcal{C}' = \{C_1', C_2', \ldots, C_{k/2}'\}$, let $C_i'=C_i\cup C_{i'}$ and let $\mathcal{C} = \{C_1, C_{1'}, C_2, C_{2'},\ldots,C_{k/2},C_{k/2'}\}$.

    Furthermore, we have that $m' = {m \choose 2}$. It follows that
    \[k'\log n' \leq \frac{k+1}{2}\log (n+1) \stackrel{k\geq 2}{\leq} \frac{3k}{4}\log (n+1) \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}k\log ((n+1)^{\sqrt{3}/2}) \stackrel{n\geq 5}{\leq} \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}k\log (n).\] 
    Note that in the first inequality, we consider the cases of $k$ being modified to be even.
    It follows that for $k>2$ the parameter decreases by at least a factor of $\sqrt{3}/{2}$ and for $k=2$ the parameter diminisher produces either a trivial yes- or a trivial no-instance.

  }

    \[k'\log n' \leq \frac{k+1}{2}\log (n+1) \stackrel{k\geq 2}{\leq} \frac{3k}{4}\log (n+1) \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}k\log ((n+1)^{\sqrt{3}/2}) \stackrel{n\geq 5}{\leq} \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}k\log (n).\] 
    Note that in the first inequality, we consider the cases of $k$ being modified to be even.
    It follows that for $k>2$ the parameter decreases by at least a factor of $\sqrt{3}/{2}$ and for $k=2$ the parameter diminisher produces either a trivial yes- or a trivial no-instance.

nodes.name: Exponential Time Hypothesis
nodes.statement:
The complexity-theoretic assumption we base our results on is the \emph{Exponential Time Hypothesis}, or ETH for short~\cite{ImpagliazzoP01,lokshtanov2011lower}.
The Exponential Time Hypothesis states that there is no algorithm for \prob{3-CNF-Sat} running in~$2^{o(n)}$ time, where $n$ denotes the number of variables.

nodes.name: No strong diminishers under ETH
nodes.statement: Assuming \textnormal{ETH}{}, none of the following problems is strongly diminishable: \pprob{$k$-CNF-Sat}{n}, \pprob{Rooted Path}{k}, \pprob{Clique}{\Delta}, \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{tw}}, and \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{bw}}.
assumptions: Assuming \textnormal{ETH}{}
conclusions: none of the following problems is strongly diminishable: \pprob{$k$-CNF-Sat}{n}, \pprob{Rooted Path}{k}, \pprob{Clique}{\Delta}, \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{tw}}, and \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{bw}}.
nodes.label: thm:main2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5
nodes.statement:
We show the statements of~\Cref{thm:main2} with several
propositions.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 5 follows from Propositions 9-11 and Corollary 4.

nodes.name: Strong diminishers speed up algorithms
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem. If there is an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that solves any instance~$(x,k)\in L$ in $2^{O(k)}\cdot |x|^{O(1)}$ time and $L$ is strongly diminishable, then there is an algorithm~$\mathcal{B}$ that solves $L$ in $2^{O(k/ f(x, k))}\cdot |x|^{f(x, k)^{O(1)}}$ time, where $f:L\to \mathbb{N}$ is a function mapping instances of $L$ to the natural numbers with the following property: For every constant $c$ there is a natural number $n$ such that for all instances $(x, k)\in L$ we have that $|x|\ge n$ implies that $f(x, k)\ge c$.
assumptions: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem.
there is an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that solves any instance~$(x,k)\in L$ in $2^{O(k)}\cdot |x|^{O(1)}$ time and $L$ is strongly diminishable
conclusions: there is an algorithm~$\mathcal{B}$ that solves $L$ in $2^{O(k/ f(x, k))}\cdot |x|^{f(x, k)^{O(1)}}$ time
nodes.statement_short: A strong diminisher turns a $2^{O(k)}$ algorithm into a $2^{O(k/f)}|x|^{f^{O(1)}}$ one for any unbounded $f$.
nodes.label: lem:strdim

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an algorithm that solves any instance~$(x,k)\in L$ in~$2^{c_1\cdot k}\cdot |x|^{c_2}$~time with constants $c_1,c_2>0$ and let~$\mathcal{D}$ be a strong parameter diminisher for $L$ with constant~$d\geq 2$. Recall that by definition of a strong parameter diminisher, the size of the instance grows at most polynomially each time $\mathcal{D}$ is applied. Let $b\geq 1$ be a constant such that the size of the instance obtained by applying $\mathcal{D}$ once to $(x,k)$ is upper-bounded by $|x|^b$. We set~$c:=\min\{2,b\}$. Let~$f:L\to\mathbb{N}$ be a function such that $f(x, k)\ge c$ for all $(x, k)\in L$ with $|x|\ge c_0$ for some constant~$c_0\in\mathbb{N}$. Let $(x',k')$ be the instance of $L$ obtained by applying $\mathcal{D}$ $\lceil\log_{c} f(x,k)\rceil$ times to instance~$(x,k)\in L$ with $|x|\geq c_0$. We obtain \[ |x'| \leq |x|^{b^{\lceil\log_{c} f(x,k)\rceil}} \leq |x|^{b^{2\log_{c} f(x,k)}} \leq |x|^{f(x,k)^{c_3}},\, \text{for some constant $c_3\geq 1$.} \] Furthermore, the parameter decreases by the constant factor~$d$ each time the diminisher is applied, hence \[ k' = k/d^{\lceil\log_{c} f(x,k)\rceil}\leq k/d^{\log_{c} f(x,k)} \leq k/d^{\log_{d} f(x,k)}\leq k/f(x,k) . \] Finally, applying $\mathcal{A}$ on $(x', k')$ solves $(x',k')$ in time \[2^{c_1\cdot k'}\cdot |x'|^{c_2} \leq 2^{c_1\cdot k/f(x,k)}\cdot |x|^{c_2\cdot f(x,k)^{c_3}} \in 2^{O(k/ f(x,k))}\cdot |x|^{f(x,k)^{O(1)}}.\qedhere\]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the strong diminisher $\lceil\log_c f\rceil$ times, then run $\mathcal{A}$; bound size and parameter.

nodes.name: Fix algorithm and diminisher
nodes.statement:
Let $L$ be a parameterized problem. 
    Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an algorithm that solves any instance~$(x,k)\in L$ in~$2^{c_1\cdot k}\cdot |x|^{c_2}$~time with constants $c_1,c_2>0$ and let~$\mathcal{D}$ be a strong parameter diminisher for $L$ with constant~$d\geq 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\mathcal{A}$ and strong diminisher $\mathcal{D}$.

nodes.name: Size growth
nodes.statement: Recall that by definition of a strong parameter diminisher, the size of the instance grows at most polynomially each time $\mathcal{D}$ is applied.
nodes.statement_short: Recall instance size grows polynomially per application.

nodes.name: Constants and f
nodes.statement:
Let $b\geq 1$ be a constant such that the size of the instance obtained by applying $\mathcal{D}$ once to  $(x,k)$ is upper-bounded by $|x|^b$.
    We set~$c:=\min\{2,b\}$.
    Let~$f:L\to\mathbb{N}$ be a function such that $f(x, k)\ge c$ for all $(x, k)\in L$ with $|x|\ge c_0$ for some constant~$c_0\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $b$, $c$ and $f$.

nodes.name: Size bound
nodes.statement:
Let $(x',k')$ be the instance of $L$ obtained by applying $\mathcal{D}$ $\lceil\log_{c} f(x,k)\rceil$ times to instance~$(x,k)\in L$ with $|x|\geq c_0$.
  
    We obtain 
    \[ |x'| \leq |x|^{b^{\lceil\log_{c} f(x,k)\rceil}} \leq |x|^{b^{2\log_{c} f(x,k)}} \leq |x|^{f(x,k)^{c_3}},\, \text{for some constant $c_3\geq 1$.} \]

nodes.name: Parameter bound
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, the parameter decreases by the constant factor~$d$ each time the diminisher is applied, hence 
    \[ k' = k/d^{\lceil\log_{c} f(x,k)\rceil}\leq  k/d^{\log_{c} f(x,k)} \leq k/d^{\log_{d} f(x,k)}\leq k/f(x,k) . \]
nodes.statement_short: $k'\le k/f(x,k)$.

nodes.name: Running time
nodes.statement:
Finally, applying $\mathcal{A}$ on $(x', k')$ solves $(x',k')$ in time 
    \[2^{c_1\cdot k'}\cdot |x'|^{c_2} \leq  2^{c_1\cdot k/f(x,k)}\cdot |x|^{c_2\cdot f(x,k)^{c_3}} \in 2^{O(k/ f(x,k))}\cdot |x|^{f(x,k)^{O(1)}}.\qedhere\]
nodes.statement_short: Running $\mathcal{A}$ gives the claimed time.

nodes.name: k-CNF-Sat and Rooted Path are diminishable (Chen, Flum, Müller)
nodes.statement: Chen, Flum, and M\"{u}ller~\cite{chen2011lower} showed that \pprob{$k$-CNF-Sat}{n} and \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} are diminishable.

nodes.name: k-CNF-Sat is not strongly diminishable under ETH
nodes.statement: Assuming \textnormal{ETH}{}, \pprob{$k$-CNF-Sat}{n} is not strongly diminishable.
assumptions: Assuming \textnormal{ETH}{}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 9
nodes.statement: \prob{$k$-CNF-Sat} can be solved in $O^*(2^{n})$ time via a brute-force algorithm~$\mathcal{A}$, but does not admit a~$2^{o(n)}$ time algorithm under the~\textnormal{ETH}{}. By \Cref{lem:strdim} with algorithm~$\mathcal{A}$ and~$f(\phi)=\log n$, \pprob{$k$-CNF-Sat}{n} does not admit a strong parameter diminisher unless the~\textnormal{ETH}{} breaks.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4 with brute force and $f=\log n$ would give a $2^{o(n)}$ algorithm.

nodes.name: Rooted Path is not strongly diminishable under ETH
nodes.statement: Assuming \textnormal{ETH}{}, \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} is not strongly diminishable.
assumptions: Assuming \textnormal{ETH}{}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10
nodes.statement: \prob{Hamiltonian Path} on an $n$-vertex graph reduces trivially to \prob{Rooted Path} by adding a universal vertex and taking it as the root and setting the length of the path $k=n$. As \prob{Hamiltonian Path} does not admit a $2^{o(n)}$ time algorithm unless the~\textnormal{ETH}{} breaks~\cite{lokshtanov2011lower}, \prob{Rooted Path} does not admit a~$2^{o(n)}$ time algorithm unless the~\textnormal{ETH}{} breaks. There is an algorithm for \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} running in $2^{O(k)}\mathrm{poly}(n)$ time~\cite{AlonYZ95}. Let $(G=(V,E), k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} and set~$f(G, k)=\log(|V|)=\log n$. By \Cref{lem:strdim} we get an algorithm for \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} running in~$2^{O(k/\log n)}\cdot |G|^{(\log n)^{O(1)}}\in 2^{o(n)}$ time. Hence, \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} does not admit a strong parameter diminisher unless the~\textnormal{ETH}{} breaks.
nodes.statement_short: Hamiltonian Path reduces to Rooted Path; Lemma 4 with $f=\log n$ and color coding would give a $2^{o(n)}$ algorithm.

nodes.name: ETH lower bound
nodes.statement:
\prob{Hamiltonian Path} on an $n$-vertex graph reduces trivially to \prob{Rooted Path} by adding a universal vertex and taking it as the root and setting the length of the path $k=n$.
 As \prob{Hamiltonian Path} does not admit a $2^{o(n)}$ time algorithm unless the~\textnormal{ETH}{} breaks~\cite{lokshtanov2011lower}, \prob{Rooted Path} does not admit a~$2^{o(n)}$ time algorithm unless the~\textnormal{ETH}{} breaks.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce Hamiltonian Path to Rooted Path; Rooted Path has no $2^{o(n)}$ algorithm under ETH.

nodes.name: Known algorithm
nodes.statement: There is an algorithm for \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} running in $2^{O(k)}\mathrm{poly}(n)$ time~\cite{AlonYZ95}.
nodes.statement_short: Color coding gives $2^{O(k)}\mathrm{poly}(n)$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Let $(G=(V,E), k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} and set~$f(G, k)=\log(|V|)=\log n$. By \Cref{lem:strdim} we get an algorithm for \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} running in~$2^{O(k/\log n)}\cdot |G|^{(\log n)^{O(1)}}\in 2^{o(n)}$ time.
nodes.statement_short: With $f=\log n$ get a $2^{o(n)}$ algorithm.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} does not admit a strong parameter diminisher unless the~\textnormal{ETH}{} breaks.
nodes.statement_short: No strong diminisher unless ETH fails.

nodes.name: Clique by bandwidth is not strongly diminishable under ETH
nodes.statement: Assuming \textnormal{ETH}{}, \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{bw}} is not strongly diminishable.
assumptions: Assuming \textnormal{ETH}{}
nodes.label: prop:ethcliquebw

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 11
nodes.statement: \prob{Clique} can be solved in $O^*(2^{\mathrm{bw}})$ time via a dynamic programming (brute-force) algorithm~$\mathcal{A}$, but does not admit a $2^{o(n)}$ time algorithm under \textnormal{ETH}{}~\cite{lokshtanov2011lower}. Note that $\mathrm{bw}(G)\in O(n)$. By \Cref{lem:strdim} with algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ and $f(G, k)=\log(|V|)=\log n$, \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{bw}} does not admit a strong parameter diminisher unless the~\textnormal{ETH}{} breaks.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4 with the $O^*(2^{\mathrm{bw}})$ algorithm and $f=\log n$ would beat the ETH bound.

nodes.name: Algorithm and lower bound
nodes.statement: \prob{Clique} can be solved in $O^*(2^{\mathrm{bw}})$ time via a dynamic programming (brute-force) algorithm~$\mathcal{A}$, but does not admit a $2^{o(n)}$ time algorithm under \textnormal{ETH}{}~\cite{lokshtanov2011lower}. Note that $\mathrm{bw}(G)\in O(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Clique solvable in $O^*(2^{\mathrm{bw}})$, no $2^{o(n)}$ under ETH; $\mathrm{bw}\in O(n)$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 4
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lem:strdim} with algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ and $f(G, k)=\log(|V|)=\log n$, \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{bw}} does not admit a strong parameter diminisher unless the~\textnormal{ETH}{} breaks.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4 with $f=\log n$ excludes a strong diminisher.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4
nodes.statement: Since we have that $\Delta \le \mathrm{tw} \le \mathrm{bw}$, we get the following corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Follows from Proposition 11 since $\Delta\le\mathrm{tw}\le\mathrm{bw}$.

nodes.name: Clique by degree and treewidth not strongly diminishable under ETH
nodes.statement: Assuming \textnormal{ETH}{}, \pprob{Clique}{\Delta} and \pprob{Clique}{\mathrm{tw}} are not strongly diminishable.

nodes.name: Diminishability of uncolored (directed) Path
nodes.statement:
We proved that \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} is diminishable (and thus 
does not admit a strict polynomial kernel unless $\textnormal{P}{}=\textnormal{NP}{}${}). Can this
result be extended to the uncolored version of the problem?

also_stated_at: The \prob{Multicolored Path} problem is defined as follows: Given an undirected graph~$G=(V,E)$ with a vertex coloring function $\mathrm{col}: V \to \{1,\ldots,k\}$, determine whether there exists a simple path of length~$k$ with one vertex of each color.

also_stated_at: We give a strong diminisher for the \prob{Set Cover} problem: Given a set~$U$ called the universe, a family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^U$ of subsets of $U$, and an integer $k$, the question is whether there are $k$ sets in the family $\mathcal{F}$ that cover the whole universe.

nodes.name: Short Binary NTM Computation
also_stated_at: In \prob{Short Binary NTM Computation} the input Turing machines are restricted to have a two-element alphabet.

nodes.name: Short NTM Computation
also_stated_at: The \prob{Short NTM Computation} problem asks, given a Turing machine~$M$, a word $x\in\Sigma^*$ which is initially written on the tape, and a number~$k$ in unary encoding, whether there is a run such that, after $k$ computation steps, the Turing machine $M$ is in an accepting state.
